title: College Athletes as Employees
resolution: Resolved: College athletes should be classified as employees of their universities.
summary: College athletes can now earn money from endorsements, and schools can share revenue with them. Should they go further and be treated as employees, with wages and the right to bargain?

background.p: For decades the NCAA barred college athletes from being paid beyond scholarships. Since 2021, athletes have been allowed to earn money from their name, image and likeness (NIL) through endorsements and sponsorships. In June 2025 a federal judge approved the settlement in *House v. NCAA*, which provides about $2.8 billion in back damages to former athletes and lets schools share athletic revenue directly with players, up to a cap of $20.5 million per school in 2025–26, rising each year. It also replaced scholarship limits with roster limits, which cost some walk-on and partial-scholarship athletes their spots.

The settlement did not decide whether athletes are employees, which would bring wages, workplace protections, taxes and possibly union bargaining. Supporters of employee status say athletes work long hours generating billions; opponents worry it would end the student-athlete model, force cuts to sports that don't earn money, and create problems under Title IX, the law requiring equal opportunity for women in school sports.

disputed.q: Would employee status force schools to cut sports?
positions: Opponents expect schools to cut sports that don't earn money if they must pay wages and benefits to all athletes.
Supporters say most money flows in football and basketball, and schools have choices about coaches' salaries and facilities.

terms.def: Name, image and likeness: athletes' right to earn money from endorsements and appearances.
Schools paying part of their athletic revenue directly to athletes, as allowed under the House settlement.
The 1972 federal law banning sex discrimination in education programs, including athletics.
Negotiation between employers and a union representing employees.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Athletes who do the work that brings in billions should have the rights and pay of employees.

args.claim: Athletes perform work that generates large revenue.
args.warrant: Long practice hours, travel and games produce media and ticket revenue for schools; people doing that work should be treated as workers.
args.evidence: Athletic department revenue data; time-demand surveys of athletes; the size of the House settlement.
args.response: The negative answers that most college sports lose money, and athletes are students first.

args.warrant: Employees get workplace safety rules, injury coverage and the right to bargain; athletes with serious injuries can be left with little support.
args.evidence: Labor law protections; cases of athletes' long-term injuries and medical costs.
args.response: The negative replies that schools can provide health coverage and protections without employee status.

args.claim: Revenue sharing alone leaves athletes without a voice.
args.warrant: Schools and conferences set the terms of revenue sharing; only collective bargaining gives athletes a say in rules, pay and schedules.
args.evidence: Terms of the House settlement set without an athletes' union; examples from professional leagues.
args.response: The negative argues that bargaining across hundreds of schools would be unworkable and costly.

args.claim: The old amateur model treated athletes unfairly.
args.warrant: Coaches and administrators earned millions while athletes couldn't be paid, which courts found violated antitrust law.
args.evidence: O'Bannon v. NCAA (Ninth Circuit, 2015), which found the NCAA's ban on paying athletes for the use of their names and images violated antitrust law; the House settlement's back damages.
args.response: The negative answers that NIL and revenue sharing already fix this without turning students into employees.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Athletes should be paid fairly, but as student-athletes, not employees.

args.claim: Employee status could lead schools to cut sports.
args.warrant: Most college teams don't make money; adding wages, benefits and taxes may push schools to cut sports such as swimming, wrestling and track.
args.evidence: Athletic department budgets; roster cuts that followed the House settlement.
args.response: The affirmative answers that schools could reduce spending on coaches' salaries and facilities instead.

args.claim: It creates conflicts with Title IX.
args.warrant: If most pay goes to football and men's basketball players, schools may face claims that they're failing to provide equal opportunity to women athletes.
args.evidence: Title IX challenges filed against the House settlement by women athletes.
args.response: The affirmative replies that Title IX can be applied to pay just as it is to scholarships.

args.warrant: College sports exist within education; making athletes employees could subordinate classes to work demands.
args.evidence: Graduation data for athletes; NCAA academic requirements.
args.response: The affirmative argues that work demands already dominate for many athletes, so recognizing reality is more honest.

args.claim: New pay systems already address fairness.
args.warrant: NIL deals and revenue sharing put money in athletes' hands without the legal complications of employment.
args.evidence: The House settlement's revenue-sharing cap; NIL earnings data.
args.response: The affirmative replies that these leave athletes without protections or bargaining rights.

strawmen.strawman: They want to turn college sports into the NFL.
strawmen.why: Supporters want rights and protections for athletes, not necessarily professional leagues.
strawmen.steelman: Athletes do work that generates billions; employee status would give them pay, injury protections and a voice through bargaining.

strawmen.strawman: They don't think athletes deserve anything.
strawmen.why: Most opponents support NIL and revenue sharing.
strawmen.steelman: Athletes should be paid through NIL and revenue sharing, but employee status could cut sports, create Title IX conflicts and undermine the student part of student-athlete.

weak.arg: Every college athlete brings in millions.
weak.why: Most programs and athletes don't generate large revenue.
Courts and the House settlement have already moved past this; argue about employment specifically.
